newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - Exporters call crisis talks on NZ$ surge.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Exporters call crisis talks on NZ$ surge.

text.p: A strong currency should reflect a healthy economy but New Zealand exporters say the value of the Kiwi dollar is choking them out of business.

Exasperated by the Kiwi's continued appreciation against the currencies of New Zealand's major trading partners, five key exporter groups have called for an economic summit before Christmas to address the crisis.
"It's having quite an extraordinary effect on us," said Malcolm Burns, managing director of BHP NZ Steel.
"There must be lots of export-orientated businesses that are really in deep trouble now. I personally question the management of the economy that's allowing it to happen."
New Zealand's obsession with price stability, lauded around the world, has pushed up interest rates and the value of the currency to keep inflationary pressures at bay.
The central bank is mandated to keep core inflation within a zero to two percent target band and has implemented tight monetary policy to achieve it.
KIWI APPRECIATED 21 PERCENT IN THREE YEARS
In the last three years, the Kiwi has appreciated 21 percent on a trade-weighted basis. On Friday it was trading just under 71 U.S. cents and more than 90 Australian cents.

Burns said that if the Kiwi goes up by 10 percent, it costs BHP NZ Steel NZ$25 million a year. "That's ignoring the effect on domestic prices. It's not only potentially export revenue loss, it is also a domestic revenue loss," he said.
One glance at the recent round of company profit results shows just how much the manufacturing, agricultural and export sectors are feeling the pinch of the soaring currency.

On Tuesday, the New Zealand Dairy Board described the rising value of the Kiwi as a "billion-dollar burden". Its chairman said the cumulative effect of the Kiwi's appreciation over the last three years was to wipe NZ$1.1 billion off earnings over that period.
A week ago, wool industry executives said New Zealand's productive sector was being "skinned alive" by the continuing rise in the value of the dollar.

Air New Zealand said the stronger dollar had reduced receipts from overseas sales in foreign currencies by around NZ$100 million in the year to June, despite a 3.3 percent rise in international passenger revenues.
A plethora of smaller companies are seeing their profits swallowed by the surging currency.
"The evidence is that it is at the present time overvalued, some say by as much as 10 percent," said Simon Arnold, chief executive of the Manufacturers Federation.
"If you look at the forces that are holding it up, it is partly a consequence of monetary conditions, but I think it's also the kind of government you're likely to see."
A new administration has yet to emerge from last month's inconclusive election, the first under a new system of proportional representation.

The main political parties are still pounding out coalition arrangements, but whatever the outcome, the government will be of a centrist persuasion and is likely to loosen the purse strings to meet pre-election promises.
Looser fiscal policy is inflationary, and exporters fear that may reduce the likelihood of an easing in monetary policy.

"It's a fair old bet that you will have looser fiscal conditions. So the dollar's going up and you'd be dopey not to be buying dollars at the present time," said Arnold, whose Federation is one of the exporter groups planning a summit on the strength of the dollar.
RELAXATION IN MONETARY POLICY HELPS INVESTMENT
They say exporters badly need a relaxation in monetary policy as a signal to continue investment.
"Inevitably, if you don't continue to get the profitability, you don't get the investment, you don't get the growth, and that's a cycle that starts to come back into labour," said Arnold.
BHP NZ Steel says it will reduce its workforce by 25 percent or more between now and the middle of next year.

Two months ago, confectioner Arnotts relocated its biscuit-making to Australia, shedding 230 jobs. A month before that, livestock eartag manufacturer Allflex relocated 130 manufacturing jobs overseas.
That followed hard on the heels of Cedenco Foods transferring its tomato paste operations to Australia and chopping 500 fulltime and seasonal jobs.

"There are all sorts of reasons...but the longer manufacturers have these experiences of routinely getting burnt by an overvalued currency, they will decide to locate outside New Zealand," said Peter Harris, Council of Trade Unions economist.
"The problem that we've got is that the Reserve Bank uses the exchange rate as its primary transmission mechanism in controlling inflation."

It is a message that has fallen largely on deaf ears, until now. Keen to remain in favour while coalition talks drag on, politicians from both of the parties that could lead the next government have declared the dollar overvalued.
But neither the conservative National Party, which currently heads a caretaker government, nor the main opposition Labour Party have said explicitly how they aim to clip its wings.

Exporters point out that although inflationary pressures are predominantly to be found in the non-tradeables sector, monetary policy is non-discriminating, clobbering them for price rises they have nothing to do with.
"The answer to how they handle it can't come from a simple steel maker," said Burns. "But they really do have to take their blinkers off a bit."
